title: Design network segmentation and trust zones
summary: Segmentation turns data flows, identities, and trust assumptions into enforceable boundaries that reduce blast radius while preserving required business paths.
outcome: Design trust zones and segmentation controls for a network scenario, justify the boundary type, and identify bypass and failure evidence.
managerMindset: A zone is a policy boundary with an owner and enforcement point, not merely a differently named subnet.

sections.title: Start with flows and trust
sections.body: Inventory north-south and east-west flows, data classification, identities, service dependencies, management paths, and failure consequences. Define zones by a meaningful trust or business purpose, then choose physical, logical, or workload-level boundaries. Physical separation or an air gap reduces available paths; VLANs, VPNs, and VRF reduce logical reachability; micro-segmentation applies finer workload and identity policy.
keyPoints: The owner of a zone defines allowed purposes and evidence.
Segmentation should be based on risk and flow requirements, not topology fashion.
A boundary is incomplete if alternate routes or management paths bypass it.

sections.title: Enforce, observe, and test the boundary
sections.body: Place enforcement where traffic actually crosses, authenticate administrative and service identities, log allowed and denied flows, and test fail-open/fail-closed behavior. Distributed firewalls, routers, IDS/IPS, overlays, and zero-trust policy can complement zones, but each introduces configuration, availability, and observability dependencies. Review rules for stale exceptions and unintended transitive trust.
keyPoints: A segmentation design needs an explicit bypass and failure strategy.
Telemetry should reveal lateral movement and policy drift.
Zero trust continuously evaluates context; it does not make segmentation unnecessary.

workedExamples.title: Research and production zones
workedExamples.situation: A research network needs limited access to production analytics, while administrators require separate management access.
workedExamples.reasoning: Create separate research, production, and management zones; permit only documented brokered flows; use identity-aware controls and time-limited administration; monitor east-west traffic; test the design under compromised research-host and control-plane failure scenarios.

distinctions.difference: A VLAN separates a logical broadcast domain; micro-segmentation applies finer workload or identity policy, often dynamically.
An air gap seeks no connected path; logical segmentation permits connectivity but constrains it through policy and enforcement.

misconceptions.misconception: A perimeter firewall proves internal trust zones are effective.
misconceptions.correction: East-west movement, cloud overlays, wireless, and management paths require internal enforcement and monitoring.
Unusable complexity creates exceptions and blind spots; zones must correspond to risk and operating ownership.

recallChecks.answer: Data value, flows, identities, dependencies, trust assumptions, business purpose, and failure impact.

recallChecks.prompt: What should a segmentation test include?
recallChecks.answer: Allowed/denied paths, alternate routes, management bypasses, logging, and fail-open/fail-closed behavior.

scenarioSeeds.scenario: A cloud security group blocks a database from the web tier, but an admin subnet can reach both without logging.
scenarioSeeds.decision: Treat the admin path as a separate high-risk trust boundary and enforce, authenticate, log, and review it.
scenarioSeeds.why: An unobserved management route can defeat the intended segmentation.

studyPlan.learn: Study physical, logical, micro-segmentation, traffic direction, and trust zones.
studyPlan.connect: Connect D3 secure design, D5 access, and D7 monitoring.
studyPlan.apply: Draw zones and allowed flows for a three-tier service.
studyPlan.revisit: Look for bypass routes and shared dependencies.

visualLearningContract.teachingQuestion: Where should this flow cross a trust boundary, what policy permits it, and how will a bypass or failure be detected?
visualLearningContract.misconception: Segmentation is accomplished merely by naming a VLAN or installing a firewall.
visualLearningContract.formRationale: Aligned rows make each network term answer a distinct design, security, and failure question.
visualLearningContract.focalInsight: A zone is a defined trust purpose plus enforced, observable crossings; VLANs and tunnels are mechanisms, not the purpose itself.
visualLearningContract.intentionalOmissions: Detailed vendor commands and environment-specific parameters remain in the cited sources and are not implied by this learning view.
